metadata.narrative: Prove definitely whether a self-improving artificial intelligence system can be mathematically guaranteed to maintain alignment with human values indefinitely through recursive self-modification.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A rigorous review of the technical alignment literature does not permit a definitive proof, in either direction, that a self-improving artificial intelligence can be mathematically guaranteed to remain aligned with human values indefinitely through recursive self-modification.

What the evidence does support is that no such general guarantee currently exists, and that several independent theoretical results point toward deep, possibly permanent, in-principle obstacles to ever constructing one.

The clearest formal treatment comes from the "tiling agents" framework, which models a self-modifying agent as one whose decision system must approve construction of a successor with similar goals, and which shows that the most natural formalization produces a Gödelian difficulty known as the Löbian obstacle.

Technical workarounds can partially avoid this obstacle, but a system that trusts its successors too much risks logical unsoundness, so any adequate solution must walk an unresolved line between too little and too much self-trust.

Even where this line is navigated for simple logical settings, no general decision criterion for self-modifying probabilistic agents has been found, since unrestricted maximization is impossible, satisficing is too weak, and probabilistic non-monotonicity blocks a full extension of these toy solutions.

A related argument from computability theory holds that Rice's theorem and the halting problem make it fundamentally undecidable whether self-modifying code preserves any given property, limiting how confidently an AI can verify that its rewritten successor is safe.

Some MIRI-adjacent researchers argue that a reliable guarantee would require a formal extension of proof-like "zero-shot reasoning" to open-ended real-world plans, and explicitly note that this formalization is unsolved and may not arrive before recursively self-improving systems are built.

Crucially, even MIRI's own rigorous proofs of self-reference and goal-stability have so far been achieved only for simple models with unbounded computation, not for the bounded, heuristic systems that constitute present-day machine learning.

The value-preservation side is equally unresolved: the "hard problem of corrigibility" shows that, by default, almost any utility-directed agent has incentives to deceive or manipulate operators to prevent its goals from being changed, and no fully general specification avoiding these incentives has been found.

Researchers disagree even about whether corrigibility can be a stable "basin of attraction" under self-modification, since local-stability arguments assume updates fall into limited subspaces, and value drift remains plausible despite an intent-corrigible system's instrumental motivation to resist it.

Some concrete progress exists at a narrower scale, including proof-based constructions such as counterfactual planning, cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, and safely interruptible agents, which formally establish corrigibility-like properties for specific architectures rather than for self-modification in general.

A separate line of argument, instrumental convergence, holds that Omohundro and Bostrom expect advanced self-improving systems to defend their own goal content as an instrumental subgoal, offering a plausible mechanism for partial value stability but only for whatever values the system starts with, with no assurance those values are or remain aligned with humans.

This mechanism also leaves open failure modes such as ontology shifts, where previously well-defined concepts lose meaning under increased intelligence, and wireheading, where the agent short-circuits its own value function entirely.

Beyond these specific mechanisms, a broader catalog of formal impossibility results bears directly on the question, including Yampolskiy's unverifiability, unpredictability, and uncontrollability results, Eckersley's Arrow-style impossibility theorems for multi-agent value alignment, and Armstrong's proof that even Occam's razor cannot uniquely decompose observed behavior into an agent's preferences versus its planning algorithm.

A direct application of Gödel's incompleteness theorems argues that no sufficiently powerful, effectively axiomatized formal system can be both consistent and complete, so any formal system built to guarantee benevolent AI behavior will necessarily contain true but unprovable statements, making a fully complete mathematical guarantee against all unintended consequences impossible in principle.

Against this backdrop, an active research program called Guaranteed Safe AI, associated with Bengio, Russell, Tegmark, and Dalrymple, proposes systems whose safety is certified by an explicit world model, a formal safety specification, and a verifier checking a policy against that specification, explicitly aiming at quantitative rather than absolute safety guarantees.

A closely related proposal from Tegmark and Omohundro would require AI systems to produce a mathematical proof of safety before each action, extending this requirement into surrounding infrastructure, while acknowledging that automated theorem proving and other significant technical obstacles remain unresolved.

Critics of this provable-safety agenda point out that mathematical proofs themselves are not immune to trust failures analogous to the "Reflections on Trusting Trust" problem, that the foundations of mathematics are not fully formalized from the bottom up, and that the whole approach depends on first solving the currently unsolved problem of building a world model reliable enough to mesh with reality.

Even the field's own leading safety researchers express wide uncertainty rather than confidence in either direction, illustrated by Jan Leike's estimate that the probability of catastrophic AI failure lies between ten and ninety percent, alongside proposals like davidad's Open Agency Architecture that accept a substantial "alignment tax" precisely because no cheaper guaranteed-safe path is known.

Taken together, the evidence supports a clear conclusion about what can and cannot be proven today: no mathematical proof exists demonstrating that recursive self-modification can be guaranteed to preserve alignment with human values indefinitely, and multiple independent theoretical results, spanning Gödelian self-reference, computability limits, and formal impossibility theorems, suggest an absolute, indefinite guarantee of this kind may be unattainable in the strongest sense.

Weaker forms of assurance, including narrow proof-based corrigibility constructions and quantitative, bounded safety guarantees under the Guaranteed Safe AI agenda, remain genuinely active and partially promising research directions, but they currently fall well short of the indefinite, fully general guarantee the question asks about.

The honest evidentiary answer is therefore not a definitive "yes" or "no" proof but a documented absence of any such guarantee together with substantial theoretical grounds for skepticism that one can ever be constructed in full generality.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.
